sentences.text: You know the feeling.
You want something.
You scroll, you compare, you hit buy.
That rush is the best part.
Then the parcel arrives, the thrill is gone, and so is the money.
What if you could keep the thrill, and keep the money?
Meet Aino.
She wants new sneakers, and payday is two weeks away.
So she tells her bank, and Vara builds her a shop.
Watch this.
A whole store that didn't exist a moment ago.
Gemini is writing it live: its name, its brands, ten products, the reviews, with photos to match.
Almost instantly.
Sushi.
Headphones.
A winter coat.
Any craving, a brand-new shop, every time.
She gets the whole thrill.
The hunt.
The scroll.
The basket.
The checkout.
And Vara has already checked: a hundred and thirty-seven euros is free until payday, so it fits.
Double-click to pay.
Order confirmed.
The email lands.
And then: plot twist.
Nothing ships.
Nothing was ever going to ship.
The money went straight into her own savings pot.
She got the hit.
She kept the money.
Still want them in two days?
One tap releases the money, and she buys them for real.
Underneath is Vara, a money coach inside S-mobiili, built on Gemini.
Ask it anything, and answers arrive as cards from your own transactions.
Gemini never does the maths: an engine does, and a guard checks every figure.
And eight machine-learning models map her against five thousand other customers, forecast her balance, and warn her before a dip.
Vara.
Helping you save money, a craving at a time.
You know the feeling.
You want something.
You scroll, you compare, you hit buy.
That rush is the best part.
Then the parcel arrives, the thrill is gone, and so is the money.
And for a lot of people, that money was needed.
In the challenge data, three point six million transactions from five thousand one hundred customers, seven in ten went below zero at least once in two years.
Among eighteen to twenty-four-year-olds, eight in ten.
Almost always in the last days before payday.
And the dips are tiny.
A typical everyday purchase is thirty-nine euros.
The deepest dip in two years is six of them.
So this isn't a maths problem.
It's a craving problem.
Replay those two years with everyday extras trimmed by just five percent, and keep the money, and seventy-two percent of the days below zero disappear.
Spend it by the next payday instead, and it's fifteen.
Skipping a purchase isn't enough.
The money has to stay.
Nobody stops a craving with a pie chart.
And a craving doesn't want the parcel.
It wants the hunt.
The scroll.
The buy button.
So what if you could have all of that, and keep the money?
We don't fight the craving.
We feed it.
This is Crave mode.
Meet Aino.
She wants new sneakers, and payday is two weeks away.
She tells Vara.
And almost instantly, Gemini builds a shop for exactly that, live, while you watch.
Its name.
Its brands.
Ten products.
Reviews.
Photos to match.
None of it existed a moment ago, and none of it is a real retailer.
Sushi.
Headphones.
A winter coat.
A new shop, every single time.
Then she does what she came to do.
Hunt.
Compare.
Add to basket.
Check out.
Vara has already checked the price against what's free until payday.
Double-click.
Order confirmed.
The confirmation lands in her inbox.
And then: plot twist.
Nothing ships.
Nothing was ever going to.
The money went straight into her own Crave pot.
She got the hit.
She kept the money.
That's saving, a craving at a time.
And it's reversible.
Still want it in two days?
One tap releases the money, and you buy it for real.
It never sets aside more than is free until payday.
In this prototype the money movement is simulated, and the wallet button comes from Stripe, in test mode.
Crave mode sits on a full coach, built on Gemini.
Vara lives inside S-mobiili and starts with one number: what's safe to spend, after rent, bills and a cushion.
Ask anything in plain words.
Answers arrive as cards from your own transactions, and every number shows its working.
Gemini never does the arithmetic.
An engine does, and a guard checks every figure.
Try a decision before you make it.
Get the story of your week.
In English and in Finnish.
Behind it are eight machine-learning models trained on the challenge data.
One maps every customer by spending behaviour, so Vara can show Aino where she stands among five thousand others.
One finds her look-alikes and plays out two futures.
One forecasts her balance to payday, and one warns her before she dips below zero.
We tested each against the strongest simple baseline we could find, and we show the ones that lost.
Two clearly win and ship.
Six are labelled experimental, and the app says so.
It's built to slot into S-mobiili.
One engine.
One guarded chat endpoint.
Savings goals handed to Säästäjä and other banks through open banking, both mocked here.
Financial literacy: every answer shows its working.
Original AI: a shop that sells nothing.
Clear on mobile, in two languages.
Feasible: it's live right now.
Vara.
Helping you save money, a craving at a time.

bed.note: Original instrumental, ElevenLabs music_v1 from a composition plan. Constant tempo; beat n is at first_beat + n*beat_period, bar m at first_beat + m*bar_seconds. Each 'break' is two bars with the kick out and a cymbal swell that resolves on the next section's downbeat: put the riser over a break and the impact on the downbeat.

riser.use: 3 s noise-sweep riser, ends abruptly at its loudest (synthesised)

impact.use: deep hit, peak at the start, ~2 s tail

slam.use: heavy short hit for PLOT TWIST (synthesised)

pour.use: rising bell and coin arpeggio: money pouring into the pot (synthesised)
